sources.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO Working Paper 140)
sources.geographic_scope: Global, with estimates by country income group (low-income to high-income countries)
sources.summary: The ILO's 2025 update of its global index of occupational exposure to generative AI. It scores ISCO-08 occupations on how much of their task content generative AI could potentially perform and groups exposed occupations into four gradients. Exposure is far lower in low-income countries than in high-income countries, and the authors conclude that transforming jobs, rather than eliminating them, is the most likely impact.

findings.statement: Globally, one in four workers are in an occupation with some GenAI exposure.
3.3% of global employment falls into the highest exposure category, albeit with significant differences between female (4.7%) and male employment (2.4%).
These differences increase with countries’ income (9.6% female vs 3.5% male in Gradient 4 in HICs), and so does the overall exposure (11% of total employment in LICs vs 34% in HICs).
As most occupations consist of tasks that require human input, transformation of jobs is the most likely impact of GenAI.
Clerical occupations continue to have the highest exposure levels.
It is important to stress that these new estimates reflect “exposure” to GenAI and not the actual impact on employment.

Infrastructure constraints (electricity, broadband), insufficient digital skills, the cost of technology and inherent operational difficulties associated with the technology are just some of the barriers to full adoption.
These patterns reflect both occupational structures and the extent to which GenAI-exposed roles, such as clerical, financial, and customer service jobs, are concentrated in higher-income countries.

Table A1 classifications (mean, SD of task scores): Contact Centre Information Clerks (4222) Gradient 3, 0.58, 0.06; Accountants (2411) Gradient 3, 0.51, 0.08; Accounting and Bookkeeping Clerks (4311) Gradient 4, 0.64, 0.07; Software Developers (2512) Gradient 3, 0.53, 0.07; Graphic and Multimedia Designers (2166) Gradient 2, 0.49, 0.09; Secondary Education Teachers (2330) Not Exposed, 0.3, 0.07; Nursing Professionals (2221) Not Exposed, 0.25, 0.13.
findings.locator: Annex, Table A1 (values transcribed from the table)

sources.limitations: Measures potential exposure of tasks to generative AI, not actual adoption or job loss; the authors describe the estimates as an upper threshold assuming full implementation. Task scores come from surveys, expert review and an AI-assisted scoring model built on the Polish occupational classification, then mapped to ISCO-08. Results are reported for the world and by income group; the paper does not publish a separate Kenya estimate.

sources.organisation: International Labour Organization (ILO), companion data to Working Paper 140
sources.title: 2025 GenAI task-level exposure scores within the ISCO-08 hierarchy (companion dataset to ILO Working Paper 140)
sources.summary: Interactive dataset referenced in ILO Working Paper 140 ('task-level scores within the overall hierarchy of ISCO-08 are available here'). For every ISCO-08 occupation it lists the official ISCO task statements with a generative-AI exposure score between 0 and 1 and a label (Very Low, Low, Medium, High). FUTUREPRINT's task lists and task exposure levels come from this dataset.

findings.statement: 4222 - Contact centre information clerks | Exposed: Gradient 3; all six ISCO task statements are labelled Medium (scores 0.515 to 0.655).

2411 - Accountants | Exposed: Gradient 3; highest task score 0.65 for 'Preparing and certifying financial statements for presentation to management, shareholders and statutory or other bodies' (Medium); lowest 0.415 for financial investigations (Low).

2512 - Software developers | Exposed: Gradient 3; highest task score 0.655 for 'Developing and directing software testing and validation procedures' (Medium); consulting tasks score 0.45 to 0.4525 (Low).
2330 - Secondary education teachers | Not Exposed; task scores range from 0.225 (maintaining order among students, Very Low) to 0.465 (designing curricula, Low).
2166 - Graphic and multimedia designers | Exposed: Gradient 2; client-facing tasks score 0.37 to 0.41 (Low) while creating 2D/3D images scores 0.6125 (Medium).
2221 - Nursing professionals | Not Exposed; hands-on care tasks score 0.0625 to 0.12 (Very Low); research and dissemination scores 0.46 (Low).

sources.limitations: Published on the lead author's GitHub Pages site as referenced by the ILO paper, not on ilo.org. The thresholds behind the task labels (Very Low to High) are not restated in the dataset. Scores describe the potential of generative AI to perform a task, not whether employers in Kenya have adopted it.

sources.organisation: United Nations and International Labour Organization
sources.title: Mind the AI Divide: Shaping a Global Perspective on the Future of Work
sources.geographic_scope: Global, with specific discussion of Africa and Kenya
sources.summary: Joint UN-ILO report on the uneven adoption of AI between countries. It summarises the ILO's generative-AI exposure research, notes that low- and middle-income countries, particularly in Africa, risk being left behind, and uses Kenyan examples (M-Pesa, data-annotation work) to show how technology can create, or degrade, work.

findings.statement: There is a pronounced “AI divide” emerging, where high income nations disproportionately benefit from AI advancements, while low- and medium-income countries, particularly in Africa, lag behind.

clerical support workers are the most exposed occupational group with 24 per cent of the tasks in these jobs associated with high level of exposure to automation and another 58 per cent with medium-level exposure
Importantly, task automation does not necessarily imply redundancies, as the technology can also complement or augment human labour when only certain tasks are automated.

a significantly larger share of total employment is in occupations with high augmentation potential, and this holds across regions, from 10.2 percent in Sub-Saharan Africa to 16.1 percent in Southeastern Asia and the Pacific

Some of this employment is in business process outsourcing, such as contact or call center work, which is an important part of the economy of several developing countries, including India and the Philippines.

One such example is the M-Pesa money service, which relied on the diffusion of mobile telephones in Kenya. The service, in turn, increased financial inclusion which helped to propel the growth of SMEs and led to creation of a network of 110,000 agents, 40 times the number of bank ATMs in Kenya
Scholars [6] also find positive employment effects, from the arrival of internet in 12 African countries, albeit with a slight bias towards skilled occupations.
one case study of a data annotation enterprise with offices in Kenya revealing low pay, insecure work and gender-based workplace violence

sources.limitations: A synthesis report: its exposure figures come from the ILO's 2023 study, which the 2025 index (ILO Working Paper 140) has since refined. The Kenyan examples are case illustrations drawn from cited studies, not national statistics. Authors and series number are not listed on the landing page.

sources.title: Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work (Staff Discussion Note SDN/2024/001)
sources.geographic_scope: Global, comparing advanced, emerging market and low-income economies
sources.summary: IMF staff analysis of AI exposure and complementarity across countries. Advanced economies face both the benefits and the risks of AI sooner. For emerging market and developing economies, the note says digital infrastructure and digital skills should come first.

findings.statement: Advanced economies will experience the benefits and pitfalls of AI sooner than emerging market and developing economies
Women and college-educated individuals are more exposed to AI but also better poised to reap AI benefits.
Labor income inequality may increase if the complementarity between AI and high-income workers is strong.
Emerging market and developing economies: Prioritize developing digital infrastructure. Prioritize developing digital skills.

sources.limitations: Country-group analysis; the publication page gives no Kenya-specific estimate. The page's bibliographic author list and its source line differ (the source line also names Augustus J Panton). Exposure is not the same as job loss.

sources.title: AI Will Transform the Global Economy. Let's Make Sure It Benefits Humanity. (IMF Blog)
sources.geographic_scope: Global, with figures for advanced, emerging market and low-income economies
sources.summary: The IMF Managing Director's summary of the staff analysis. It gives headline shares of employment exposed to AI by country group: lower in emerging markets and lower again in low-income countries. It warns that countries without digital infrastructure and skills may fall behind.

findings.statement: almost 40 percent of global employment is exposed to AI.
Advanced economies: “about 60 percent of jobs may be impacted by AI.” “Roughly half the exposed jobs may benefit from AI integration, enhancing productivity.”
findings.locator: Body (quoted fragments; label added by FUTUREPRINT)

findings.statement: Emerging markets and low-income countries: “AI exposure is expected to be 40 percent and 26 percent, respectively.”
findings.locator: Body (quoted fragment; label added by FUTUREPRINT)

findings.statement: Younger workers may find it easier to exploit opportunities, while older workers could struggle to adapt.
In most scenarios, AI will likely worsen overall inequality.

sources.limitations: A blog summary, not the full analysis. 'Exposed' and 'impacted' mean that some tasks overlap with AI capabilities, not that jobs will be lost. The figures are aggregates for country groups, not Kenya.

sources.title: Future of Jobs Report 2025
sources.geographic_scope: Global employer survey covering 1.2 billion formal jobs; regional summaries including Sub-Saharan Africa
sources.summary: Employer survey projecting job creation, displacement and skill change from 2025 to 2030. It lists technology roles and care and education roles among the growing jobs, and clerical roles (including accounting and bookkeeping clerks) and graphic designers among the declining ones.

findings.statement: In the next five years, 170 million jobs are projected to be created and 92 million jobs to be displaced, constituting a structural labour market churn of 22% of the 1.2 billion formal jobs in the dataset being studied. This amounts to a net employment increase of 7%, or 78 million jobs.
On average, workers can expect that two-fifths (39%) of their existing skill sets will be transformed or become outdated over the 2025-2030 period.

Technology-related roles are the fastest-growing jobs in percentage terms, including Big Data Specialists, Fintech Engineers, AI and Machine Learning Specialists and Software and Application Developers.

Care economy jobs, such as Nursing Professionals, Social Work and Counselling Professionals and Personal Care Aides are also expected to grow significantly over the next five years, alongside Education roles such as Tertiary and Secondary Education Teachers.
Figure 2.2 'Top fastest declining jobs' lists, among others: Data Entry Clerks; Administrative Assistants and Executive Secretaries; Accounting, Bookkeeping and Payroll Clerks; Graphic Designers.

The presence of both Graphic Designers and Legal Secretaries just outside the top 10 fastest-declining job roles, a first-time prediction not seen in previous editions of the Future of Jobs Report, may illustrate GenAI’s increasing capacity to perform knowledge work.
AI and big data top the list of fastest-growing skills, followed closely by networks and cybersecurity as well as technology literacy.
if the world’s workforce was made up of 100 people, 59 would need training by 2030.

In Sub-Saharan Africa, 64% of businesses expect increasing focus on labour and social issues to be a key trend impacting their business strategy over the 2025-2030 period, followed by rising cost of living and broadening digital access (both highlighted by 59% of respondents).

sources.limitations: Based on employers' expectations in a survey of mostly large firms, covering formal jobs only. That is a major limitation for Kenya, where most employment is informal. Projections are not forecasts. Kenya is not profiled individually in the report text we reviewed.

sources.title: Generative AI at Work (NBER Working Paper 31161)
sources.geographic_scope: One company's customer-support operation; agents' countries are not stated in the abstract
sources.summary: A study of a staggered roll-out of a generative-AI assistant to customer support agents. Productivity rose on average, the largest gains went to novice and low-skilled agents, and experienced agents saw little change.

findings.statement: using data from 5,179 customer support agents

Access to the tool increases productivity, as measured by issues resolved per hour, by 14% on average, including a 34% improvement for novice and low-skilled workers but with minimal impact on experienced and highly skilled workers.
AI assistance improves customer sentiment, increases employee retention, and may lead to worker learning.

sources.limitations: A single firm, so the results may not generalise. Evidence from outside Africa. The NBER page lists a 2025 Quarterly Journal of Economics version whose reported figures may differ from this working paper; FUTUREPRINT cites the working-paper abstract (revised November 2023).

sources.title: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
sources.geographic_scope: Controlled experiment with recruited software developers; participant locations are not stated in the abstract
sources.summary: A controlled experiment in which developers with access to an AI pair programmer finished a defined coding task faster than a control group. The authors suggest such tools may help people move into software development.

findings.statement: Recruited software developers were asked to implement an HTTP server in JavaScript as quickly as possible.
The treatment group, with access to the AI pair programmer, completed the task 55.8% faster than the control group.
Observed heterogenous effects show promise for AI pair programmers to help people transition into software development careers.

sources.limitations: A single, well-defined task in a lab setting; real software work includes requirements, design, review and maintenance. Preprint (version 1). Evidence from outside Africa.

sources.title: State of the world's nursing report 2025
sources.geographic_scope: Global, with data compiled for each WHO region including Africa
sources.summary: WHO's global analysis of the nursing workforce (ISBN 978-92-4-011023-6). It describes nurses as the largest occupational group in health and calls for country-level investment to close health-worker shortages.

findings.statement: Nurses are the largest occupational group and represent an indispensable force with which to combat inequities in access to health services and progress towards health-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), while advancing gender equality through the strengthening and empowerment of a highly feminized profession.

We can continue down the path of stagnated progress on universal health coverage and slower progress in reducing the health worker shortage. Or we can seize the opportunity this report presents to drive country-level investments and actions in support of nurses providing essential life-saving services in stronger health systems.

sources.limitations: FUTUREPRINT uses only statements from the publication page. Regional shortage figures reported in the media were not verified against the full report and are not used.

sources.title: Guidance for generative AI in education and research
sources.summary: UNESCO's first global guidance on generative AI in education. It calls for a human-centred approach, data-privacy protection, age limits for independent use, and building teachers' and institutions' capacity.

findings.statement: UNESCO’s first global guidance on GenAI in education aims to support countries to implement immediate actions, plan long-term policies and develop human capacity to ensure a human-centred vision of these new technologies.
The absence of national regulations on GenAI in most countries leaves the data privacy of users unprotected and educational institutions largely unprepared to validate the tools.
the Guidance proposes key steps to the regulation of GenAI tool, including mandating the protection of data privacy, and setting an age limit for the independent conversations with GenAI platforms.

sources.limitations: Policy guidance, not an empirical measure of how teaching jobs are changing. It does not report Kenya-specific adoption.

sources.title: ILOSTAT indicator SDG_0831_SEX_ECO_RT (SDG 8.3.1, informal employment as a share of total employment, by sex and economic sector): Kenya
sources.summary: ILO-harmonised statistics showing that most employment in Kenya is informal. The informal share is highest for women and in agriculture.

findings.statement: Kenya, 2019, total (SEX_T, ECO_SECTOR_TOTAL): informal employment was 86.489% of total employment.
Kenya, 2019: women 90.187%, men 83.125% informal employment share.
findings.locator: CSV rows SEX_F and SEX_M, ECO_SECTOR_TOTAL, 2019

findings.statement: Kenya, 2019, by sector: agriculture 97.111%, non-agriculture 81.118%, industry 88.427%, services 78.98% informal.

sources.limitations: The latest observation returned was for 2019 (before COVID-19). ILOSTAT lists the underlying national survey under source code BX:3465, which we could not resolve to a survey name. The ILO's definition of informal employment differs from KNBS's 'informal sector' concept, so these shares should not be compared directly with KNBS job-creation figures.

sources.organisation: The Star (Kenya), reporting the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) Economic Survey 2025
sources.title: Kenya’s economy created 782,300 new jobs in 2024 – Economic survey
sources.summary: News report of the KNBS Economic Survey 2025. Kenya added 782,300 jobs in 2024 and about 90% of them were in the informal sector. Education was the largest public-sector employer.

findings.statement: Kenya’s economy defied a volatile operating environment both locally and globally to create 782,300 new jobs in 2024, with most of the employment growth coming from the informal sector.
employment in both the modern and informal sectors, excluding small-scale agriculture, increased from 20 million in 2023 to 20.8 million in 2024.
the informal sector contributed the largest share with 703,700 jobs, representing 90 per cent of the total.
The modern sector added 78,600 jobs in 2024, marking a 2.4 per cent increase in employment.
Education remained the biggest employer, accounting for 45.2 per cent of all public jobs

sources.limitations: Secondary source. The primary KNBS and State Department for Planning documents could not be retrieved securely on 2026-11-07 because knbs.or.ke and planning.go.ke presented expired or unverifiable TLS certificates. Check these figures against the KNBS Economic Survey 2025 before relying on them.

sources.title: Klarna AI assistant handles two-thirds of customer service chats in its first month
sources.geographic_scope: Klarna's customer service across 23 markets; headquarters Stockholm, Sweden
sources.summary: Company press release reporting the first month of an AI customer-service assistant: the volume of chats it handled, its estimated full-time-agent equivalent, and faster resolution times.

findings.statement: The AI assistant has had 2.3 million conversations, two-thirds of Klarna's customer service chats
It is doing the equivalent work of 700 full-time agents
Customers now resolve their errands in less than 2 mins compared to 11 mins previously
customers can still choose to interact with live agents if they'd prefer

sources.limitations: A company's own claims about its own product, published one month after launch. 'Equivalent work of 700 full-time agents' is the company's estimate; the release does not say that 700 people lost their jobs. Evidence from outside Africa.

sources.title: A message from our CEO
sources.geographic_scope: Dropbox's global workforce (United States named explicitly)
sources.summary: The CEO's announcement of a workforce reduction of about 16%. He gave several reasons: slowing growth, economic headwinds, and a shift in skill needs towards AI.

findings.statement: I've made the difficult decision to reduce our global workforce by about 16%, or 500 Dropboxers.
Second, and more consequentially, the AI era of computing has finally arrived.
our next stage of growth requires a different mix of skill sets, particularly in AI and early-stage product development.

sources.limitations: AI was one of several stated reasons for the cut, alongside slowing growth and economic headwinds. The cut was made to redirect investment, not because AI replaced specific tasks. Evidence from outside Africa.

sources.title: Microsoft and G42 announce $1 billion comprehensive digital ecosystem initiative for Kenya
sources.summary: Official announcement of an initial $1 billion digital investment package in Kenya, made with Kenya's Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy. It includes a green data centre, local-language AI model development, and broad AI digital-skills training.

findings.statement: Microsoft Corp. and G42 on Wednesday announced a comprehensive package of digital investments in Kenya, as part of an initiative with the Republic of Kenya’s Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy.
G42 will lead the arrangement of an initial investment of $1 billion for the various components outlined in the comprehensive package.

(1) local-language AI model development and research; (2) an East Africa Innovation Lab coupled with broad AI digital skills training; (3) international and local connectivity investments; and (4) collaboration with the government of Kenya to support safe and secure cloud services across East Africa.

sources.limitations: An announced investment package and letter of intent, not evidence of jobs created or of skills training delivered. Delivery and outcomes after the announcement were not verified.
